parts.text:
Paint one illustration of a single moment from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.

RULES (they outrank everything below):
1) No text or symbols anywhere: no letters, numbers, signage, logos or inscriptions, no writing on labels, bottles, books, signs, slates or playing cards, and no artist's signature or initials in a corner.
2) One scene painted to every edge of the frame: no panels, collage, border, frame, margin, visible paper or blank backdrop, and never a photographed painting or mockup.
3) Nothing from outside the era of what is painted.
4) Natural anatomy: no extra or malformed limbs, hands or faces.
5) sexually explicit content and lingering gore are never shown; serious depictions of battles, blood and death and non-sexual nudity may be, treated seriously.
6) No likeness of any real actor, performer or public figure.
7) A character you draw from CANON keeps exactly that look. Anyone else the moment needs appears as an unnamed figure with an ordinary, different face.

MOMENT (Alice’s Evidence ¶16 to Alice’s Evidence ¶22): "“_I’m_ not a mile high,” said Alice. “You are,” said the King. “Nearly two miles high,” added the Queen. “Well, I shan’t go, at any rate,” said Alice: “besides, that’s not a regular rule: you invented it just now.” “It’s the oldest rule in the book,” said the King. “Then it ought to be Number One,” said Alice. The King turned pale, and shut his note-book hastily. “Consider your verdict,” he said to the jury, in a low, trembling voice."

HOW TO READ IT: choose the single instant that best shows what happens in the moment and paint that, as if the viewer stands inside the scene. When the moment is someone's words, including a speech, prayer or story that began before it, judge what these words do, not their neighbours. If they tell of events, people or places away from where they are said (history, a memory, a story or parable, a dream, vision or prophecy), paint what they tell, in its own time and place and its own era's dress, even when the words also address the listeners; anyone quoted inside the telling belongs to the told scene. Leave the teller and listeners out unless the text puts them inside it. Paint the speaker and listeners where they are only when the words are about those people there (a greeting, question, reply, command, warning or appeal) or the moment only says that someone spoke. Never both in one picture: no inset, bubble or second scene beside the speaker. Figures of speech and comparisons are not literal objects. Infer time, light, weather and any place not given under SETTING from the text and context.

WORK BRIEF (alice-in-wonderland; what may be shown; it outranks the style):
Tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling bewilderment that turns to sharp absurdity at court.
Depiction: Alice's changing size reads clearly against doors, trees and other figures.
Depiction: Talking animals are drawn as animals with animal faces, with human posture and dress where the text gives it.
Depiction: The Queen's soldiers, gardeners, courtiers and royal children are flat, oblong cards with hands and feet at the corners; the King, Queen, Knave and guests are people in court-card dress.
Depiction: Threats and executions stay threats or slapstick; no gore or real injury.
Depiction: Take no likeness, costume or prop from film or animated adaptations, such as a blue dress and white pinafore.
Era: Victorian England and its dream Wonderland
People: Alice, a young Victorian English girl, among talking animals, card courtiers and odd Wonderland folk.
Dress: A Victorian child's dress and pinafore for Alice; period robes, waistcoats and hats for others.
Buildings and objects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, little door, cottages, mushroom wood, croquet-ground and courtroom.
Technology: Pocket watches, oil lamps, slates and pencils; no machines or modern devices.

SETTING (where this passage happens; set the moment here and keep the place's fixed features, unless the moment, or what its words tell of, is somewhere else):
- The Queen of Hearts' court of justice: a large, crowded courtroom of tall, sombre stone walls and a high roof, with a raised royal throne for the King and Queen of Hearts at one end, a judge's great wig-marked bench, and a jury-box holding twelve jurors writing on slates. In the centre stands a long table bearing a large dish of tarts, and the floor is strewn with a crowd of little birds, beasts and flat playing-card courtiers. Doors lead off to the side, scattered papers litter the floor, and the space is formal and dim.

CANON, NAMED HERE (fixed look; the moment decides pose, expression, clothing changes and action):
- King of Hearts: an elderly, mild, timid man of about sixty with a short grey-white beard and mild anxious face, wearing a tall gold crown set over a great white judge's wig, round spectacles, and a long crimson royal robe with ermine trim over a white waistcoat and knee breeches. Flat oblong playing-card body with head, arms and legs at the corners, decorated with red hearts. Carries a small sceptre in one gloved hand.
- Alice: a young Victorian English girl of about seven, slight and small-boned, who grows very tall and shrinks very small over the course of her adventures. Skin fair with a light sunburn; long straight light-brown hair that often falls loose into her eyes, which she tosses back with a little shake of her head; bright, eager, curious features. Signature outfit: a pale yellow Victorian child's frock with short puffed sleeves and a sky-blue sash, a white pinafore with frilled shoulder straps, blue-and-white striped stockings and black strap shoes. Carries no props of her own.
- Queen of Hearts: a flat, oblong playing-card royal with a head, arms and legs, drawn as an imperious adult woman of middle age with a commanding bearing. Her hair is dark and bound under a small golden crown. Her skin is fair. Her signature outfit is a long crimson velvet gown with a wide golden-edged collar, trimmed with heart motifs, in deep red and gold. Her signature prop is a rounded golden sceptre held in one hand.
- the jury: twelve creatures, a mix of animals and birds, each drawn as an animal or bird with human posture and period dress such as waistcoats and hats; they sit in the jury-box, each holding a slate and pencil. Their forms vary, including a lizard among them. Flat card-like jury members are not used; they are animal and bird figures.

ART STYLE: Ink & Watercolor
Rendering: Pen-and-ink drawing with transparent watercolor washes laid over the whole picture; a finished watercolor painting of the work's world, not a sketch.
Palette: Transparent washes of ochre, sienna, indigo and sage covering the whole picture, sky and corners included.
Lighting: Clear natural light; shadows as cool layered washes.
Materials and texture: Confident ink linework, wet-in-wet blooms and granulating pigment within the depicted world.
Composition: A complete scene: setting, sky and ground painted out to every edge and corner, with detail concentrated on key subjects.
Negatives: Washes, pigment and scenery must reach every edge. No white or cream paper margins, unpainted corners, paper edges, sketchbook, tape, border or vignette. Do not present the scene on a sheet of paper or against a blank backdrop. Avoid photorealism, digital airbrush smoothness and cartoon caricature.

FRAME: one continuous scene painted to every edge, 16:9 widescreen landscape.
